Madhav: Before we start: rules. Two check-ins a week, ten minutes, Tuesday and Friday at lunch.
Varun: Ten minutes? That's nothing.
Madhav: That's the point. Everyone says what's done, what's next, what's stuck.
Varun: And a chat group?
Madhav: I already made "Bridge Team." One more rule: if you're stuck, say so by the next check-in. Not the day before the deadline.
Varun: What if I'm embarrassed to say I'm stuck?
Madhav: Then say "I need ten minutes of help." That's all. Nobody counts.
Varun: Fine. Actually I'm already stuck on the load table. I can't find the formula.
Madhav: See? Tuesday I'll bring my notes. Two minutes, done.
Varun: Okay. This might actually work.

qa.q: On which days are the check-ins?
qa.a: The check-ins are on Tuesday and Friday at lunch.

qa.q: How does Varun feel about admitting being stuck?
qa.a: Varun feels embarrassed at the thought, though Varun does admit being stuck on the load table.

qa.q: What could the team do if someone misses a check-in, and why?
qa.a: They could message the person in the chat that day, because an early nudge finds a problem before it becomes a deadline crisis.

qa.q: How does Madhav see a member who is stuck?
qa.a: Madhav sees it as normal and easy to fix, saying nobody counts the times, so asking for ten minutes of help is fine.

grounding: The team agrees on twice-weekly ten-minute check-ins, a common chat group and a rule that anyone stuck says so early, so problems surface before they become deadline crises.

subtype: Approach: setting shared rules and check-ins [Action]

Our Class 10 team project last year was a model of a smart streetlight, and honestly, the thing that saved it wasn't the circuit. It was a rule.

In the first meeting, Salma, who led the group, tapped her pen and said, "Two check-ins a week, Tuesday and Friday, ten minutes in the library corner. And one rule: if you're stuck, you say it the same day in the group chat. No hiding."

I'm Kiran, and I was the one who got stuck first. The light sensor wouldn't respond, and I was embarrassed to admit it. But the rule was the rule, so I posted, "Sensor dead, don't know why." Salma replied in five minutes, and Tuesday we found the wire in the wrong pin.

Without that rule I'd have fiddled alone till the last week. Instead, we submitted four days early, and I actually slept the night before.

qa.q: On which days were the check-ins?
qa.a: The check-ins were on Tuesday and Friday, ten minutes in the library corner.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel about admitting the sensor problem?
qa.a: Kiran felt embarrassed to admit being stuck, but the rule made it easier to post anyway.

qa.q: What else could the team add to their rules?
qa.a: They could add a shared list of who owns which part, so everyone knows whom to ask when something breaks.

qa.q: How might Salma see the rule working when Kiran posted?
qa.a: Salma probably felt reassured and pleased, since the rule caught the problem early and she could help within five minutes.

grounding: A reflective account of a team agreeing on short twice-weekly check-ins, a common chat and a rule to speak up early when stuck.

Mentor's note, Class 12 physics project, Group C

Naveen and Jaya's group of five began badly: in week one, two members did not know what the others were building. I suggested they agree on a routine before touching any wires.

They wrote their own rules on a chart paper and stuck it in the lab: a ten-minute check-in every Monday and Thursday at lunch; one chat group for all updates; and "if stuck, say so within a day".

In week three, Jaya posted that the motor they ordered would arrive late. Because it came out on Thursday and not the night before submission, Naveen found a spare in the junior lab.

I sat in on two check-ins. They were short, sometimes silly, but everyone spoke. I have asked the group to share their chart with the other project teams next week.

qa.q: How often did the group hold check-ins?
qa.a: They held a ten-minute check-in every Monday and Thursday at lunch.

qa.q: What might Jaya have felt when posting that the motor would be late?
qa.a: Jaya was probably worried and a little anxious about delaying everyone, but trusted the group enough to speak up.

qa.q: How could the mentor build on this group's success?
qa.a: The mentor could invite a member to explain the chart to other groups, so peers hear how early warnings saved time.

qa.q: How did the routine change things for Naveen?
qa.a: Naveen had time to find a spare motor in the junior lab, which would have been impossible if the problem had surfaced the night before.

grounding: A mentor's note shows a team agreeing on short twice-weekly check-ins, a shared chat and a rule to speak up early, which surfaces problems before deadlines.
